sections.section_title: The Fifth Trumpet -- The Star and the Abyss
sections.summary: The fifth angel sounds and a fallen star receives a key (divine passive edothe) to the bottomless pit, opening it to release smoke that darkens the sun and air, with every element operating under derivative, granted authority traceable back through the throne-Lamb-scroll-trumpet chain.

Locusts emerge from the abyss with scorpion-like power, forbidden from harming vegetation or the sealed, permitted only to torment the unsealed for five months without killing, producing agony so severe that people seek death but cannot find it.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies the purpose of the bounded, non-lethal torment as remedial rather than merely punitive: 'The purpose of the torment is not destruction but affliction -- a chastisement that, by its very refusal to allow escape through death, presses the sufferers toward another response.' That intended response is repentance (addressed in 9:20-21). If God designed the judgment to provoke a genuine human response, the design presupposes that repentance is a real capacity the sufferers possess. A judgment structured to elicit repentance is incoherent if the capacity to repent has been unilaterally withheld. The five-month limit and the prohibition against killing reinforce the conditional, opportunity-creating character of the affliction.
key_phrases: they were not permitted to kill anyone, but to torment for five months
men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them
only the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads

sections.summary: The locusts are described as a composite creature combining features of war horses, crowned figures, human faces, women's hair, lion teeth, iron breastplates, chariot-like wing-sound, and scorpion tails, drawing on Joel 1-2 and the Egyptian plague tradition to construct a symbolic vision of overwhelming, divinely authorized spiritual torment.

The locust army has a king identified as 'the angel of the abyss,' named Abaddon in Hebrew (personified Destruction, a synonym for Sheol) and Apollyon in Greek (Destroyer), with the Greek name carrying a phonetic echo of Apollo, the patron deity of the Roman emperors and a god associated with plagues.

A structural marker announces the first woe has passed and two more are coming, connecting back to the eagle's announcement of three woes in 8:13 and signaling that the trajectory of judgment is intensifying.

sections.section_title: The Sixth Trumpet -- The Four Angels at the Euphrates
sections.summary: A voice from the golden altar (the same altar that received the saints' prayers in 8:3-5) commands the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates, who had been prepared for the exact hour, day, month, and year to kill a third of mankind, with the escalation from torment-without-death (fifth trumpet) to massive killing marking a new phase of judgment still governed by the fraction 'a third.'

sections.section_title: The Cavalry of Fire, Smoke, and Brimstone
sections.summary: A cavalry of two hundred million -- exceeding the entire population of the ancient world -- rides horses with lion heads that breathe fire, smoke, and brimstone (the signature instruments of divine judgment from the Sodom tradition) and serpent-like tails, killing a third of humanity with these three plagues.

The survivors of the trumpet plagues refuse to repent either of their idolatry (worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, brass, stone, and wood 'which can neither see nor hear nor walk') or of their ethical violations (murders, sorceries, immorality, thefts), replicating the Pharaoh pattern of escalating judgment met by unyielding human obstinacy.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies these verses as 'the theological climax of the chapter': everything preceding them -- the locust torment, the killing of a third of humanity -- was designed to produce repentance. The statement 'they did not repent' (ou metenoesan, stated twice) places the operative failure squarely on the humans. The entire trumpet sequence is structured as an escalating divine demand for a human response that the humans refuse to give. The author's own argument treats repentance as something the earth-dwellers could have done but chose not to do. The neutral reading's summary makes this explicit: 'The document does not assume that its audience will automatically be among the saved; it places the choice before them with unflinching clarity.' The contrast with the assemblies (who are called to repent in 2:5, 16, 21-22; 3:3, 19) reinforces that the author treats repentance as a genuine human capacity: the assemblies can repent while opportunity exists, the earth-dwellers refuse to repent despite devastating evidence of God's power. The Pharaoh parallel introduces the hardening motif, but the neutral reading notes that the Exodus text itself alternates between Pharaoh hardening his own heart and God hardening it, and here the author attributes the failure exclusively to the humans -- 'they did not repent' -- without invoking divine hardening as a cause.
key_phrases: did not repent of the works of their hands
they did not repent of their murders nor of their sorceries nor of their immorality nor of their thefts
which can neither see nor hear nor walk
